summary: Top model interactions cluster around baseline risk (age, baseline SBP), blood pressure composition (DBP vs SBP), and kidney function (eGFR / CKD flag). SHAP means suggest older age, higher SBP, and presence of CKD increase the relative/absolute benefit of intensive SBP lowering, while higher DBP and higher eGFR are associated with reduced treatment benefit (i.e., they modify the effect of intensive therapy). The hypotheses below propose biological, pharmacological, and statistical/proxy mechanisms that could explain these heterogeneous treatment effects and suggest validation approaches.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Chronological age (years); older patients have higher baseline cardiovascular risk and different vascular physiology (arterial stiffness).
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Age modifies the tradeoff between absolute benefit and harms from intensive BP lowering. Older adults have higher baseline event rates (higher absolute potential benefit) and different vascular properties that may change how much lowering systolic BP reduces events.

mechanisms.description: Age-related arterial stiffening increases pulse pressure and systolic load; reducing systolic BP can disproportionately reduce left ventricular afterload and stroke risk in older adults, producing greater absolute cardiovascular benefit than in younger adults.

Age influences pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics (e.g., altered baroreflex sensitivity, increased sensitivity to antihypertensives), so the same SBP target may produce larger hemodynamic changes (and thus larger treatment effects) in older patients compared with younger ones.

Age is a strong proxy for baseline absolute cardiovascular risk and multimorbidity; higher baseline risk inflates absolute risk reductions from the same relative treatment effect (interaction on absolute scale), so age can appear to modify benefit even if relative effects are similar.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Elderly (e.g., ≥75) may derive greater absolute benefit from intensive SBP lowering; careful monitoring for orthostatic hypotension and adverse events is still warranted.
validation_suggestions: Pre-specified interaction test for age in RCT data (e.g., SPRINT age subgroup analyses).
Analyze absolute vs relative treatment effects by age deciles; examine event rates and adverse events (falls, syncope, AKI) separately.
Physiologic study measuring central aortic pressure / pulse pressure change with intensive therapy across age strata.
caveats: Higher absolute benefit in older adults can coexist with higher rates of adverse events; net clinical benefit depends on competing risks and frailty.
Observational age interactions may reflect survivor bias or unmeasured frailty rather than true biological modification.
Some RCT subgroup analyses (including SPRINT) showed consistent relative benefit across ages; the main difference may be absolute risk.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Diastolic blood pressure at baseline; lower DBP may indicate coronary perfusion vulnerability, while higher DBP indicates different vascular loading conditions.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Baseline DBP can modify the benefit of aggressive systolic lowering because very low DBP may increase myocardial ischemia risk when SBP is driven down further (the so‑called DBP 'J-curve'), changing net treatment effect.

mechanisms.description: Low DBP reduces coronary perfusion pressure (especially in presence of coronary artery disease); intensive lowering of SBP that further lowers DBP can precipitate myocardial ischemia, diminishing or reversing benefit on MI/cardiovascular outcomes in patients with low baseline DBP.

Antihypertensive regimens that reduce SBP substantially often lower DBP as well; patients with already low DBP may experience exaggerated reductions and adverse ischemic effects due to drug action on peripheral resistance and heart rate, altering net benefit.

Low DBP often correlates with increased arterial stiffness and older age (high pulse pressure). DBP may therefore be a proxy for vascular phenotype that interacts with therapy: worse vascular stiffness predicts poorer relative benefit from further BP reduction for certain outcomes.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients with low baseline DBP (or high pulse pressure) may experience less benefit or higher risk from intensive SBP targets; consider individualized targets and monitoring for ischemic symptoms.
validation_suggestions: Test interaction between baseline DBP (and pulse pressure) and treatment assignment on MI and composite endpoints in trial data with continuous DBP modeling.
Examine incidence of peri-treatment myocardial ischemia/ECG changes or troponin elevations across DBP strata.
Conduct mediation analyses to separate effects attributable to DBP change vs. baseline vascular stiffness.
caveats: DBP interactions are sensitive to collinearity with age, SBP, and pulse pressure; careful multivariable modeling is required.
Evidence for a causal DBP J-curve comes largely from observational and post-hoc analyses; randomized evidence is limited.
Differential measurement error in DBP (e.g., cuff technique) could distort apparent interaction.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (kidney function). Higher eGFR indicates better renal function; lower eGFR indicates CKD and higher baseline risk of CVD and drug-related harms.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Kidney function can change both the magnitude of cardiovascular risk reduction from BP lowering and the balance of harms (AKI, electrolyte disturbances). The model suggests higher eGFR reduces apparent treatment benefit (i.e., lower eGFR -> more benefit).

mechanisms.description: Reduced eGFR marks patients with systemic atherosclerosis and volume/pressure dysregulation; these patients have higher baseline cardiovascular event rates and may therefore gain greater absolute benefit from intensive BP lowering.

Impaired renal function alters clearance and sensitivity to some antihypertensives (e.g., ACE inhibitors/ARBs, certain diuretics), potentially changing achieved BP response, side‑effect profile, and net efficacy of intensive regimens.

eGFR is a proxy for multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and healthcare intensity; lower eGFR may select patients with higher baseline event risk and closer follow-up (higher ascertainment), producing an apparent interaction.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients with reduced eGFR (CKD) may realize larger absolute reductions in CVD events with intensive SBP lowering but also higher rates of renal adverse events; net benefit must consider both.
validation_suggestions: Examine RCT subgroup analyses for interaction between continuous eGFR and treatment effect on cardiovascular endpoints and AKI/decline in eGFR.
Stratify by CKD stage and evaluate absolute vs relative risk reductions and adverse event rates.
Pharmacokinetic analyses of common antihypertensives in varying eGFR ranges to assess differential drug exposure and BP response.
caveats: Apparent larger benefit at low eGFR could reflect higher baseline risk (interaction on absolute not relative scale).
Reduced eGFR also increases susceptibility to harms (AKI, hyperkalemia), so net clinical benefit may not be greater despite larger absolute CVD risk reduction.
Measurement variability in creatinine/eGFR and competing risk of death can bias interaction estimates.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Baseline systolic blood pressure. Higher baseline SBP provides more room for reduction and may predict larger absolute cardiovascular risk reduction with intensive SBP targeting.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Baseline SBP determines both how much SBP can be lowered and the baseline risk attributable to elevated SBP; higher baseline SBP is expected to amplify benefit from intensive lowering.

mechanisms.description: Higher baseline SBP is directly causally linked to vascular damage and CVD events; reducing a higher SBP yields greater immediate reduction in strain on vasculature and heart, producing larger event reductions.

Patients with higher SBP often have greater BP responsiveness to antihypertensive therapy (greater absolute reductions achievable), so the intensive arm attains larger absolute SBP drops and more outcome benefit.

Baseline SBP correlates with unmeasured risk factors (longstanding hypertension, end-organ damage); it therefore acts as a proxy for those risks and magnifies observed treatment-effect heterogeneity, particularly on the absolute scale.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients with higher baseline SBP are more likely to gain substantial absolute benefit from intensive SBP lowering; lower-baseline-SBP patients may have smaller absolute gains and greater relative risk of harms.
validation_suggestions: Model continuous interaction between baseline SBP and treatment assignment, reporting both relative and absolute risk reductions.
Subgroup analyses by baseline SBP strata (e.g., <140, 140–159, ≥160) for event rates and adverse events.
Pooling trial-level data in meta-analysis to assess whether baseline SBP modifies relative vs absolute effects.
caveats: Higher baseline SBP may increase apparent benefit on absolute scale while relative effects remain similar.
Regression to the mean and differential measurement error in SBP can bias interaction estimates.
Clinical decisions should also account for patient comorbidities and tolerability, not just baseline SBP.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Binary indicator of pre-existing chronic kidney disease. Captures clinician-diagnosed CKD or meeting diagnostic threshold separate from continuous eGFR.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: A CKD label selects a group with higher cardiovascular risk and different treatment considerations (drug selection, monitoring). The model suggests CKD presence increases the benefit of intensive therapy, consistent with higher baseline risk or differential responsiveness.

mechanisms.description: CKD is associated with accelerated atherosclerosis, inflammation, and volume/pressure dysregulation; intensive SBP lowering may more effectively reduce cardiac and cerebrovascular events in this higher‑risk biology.

CKD patients are often on regimens (e.g., diuretics, ACEi/ARB) where intensive strategies produce different hemodynamic and natriuretic effects, potentially altering both efficacy and side-effect profiles relative to non-CKD patients.

The CKD flag likely captures more than eGFR alone (diagnosis coding, nephrology involvement, medication changes) and therefore may be a proxy for closer monitoring or more aggressive management—factors that can amplify observed treatment benefit.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Patients with diagnosed CKD may gain larger absolute cardiovascular benefit from intensive SBP lowering but require careful monitoring for renal adverse events; individualized risk-benefit assessment is necessary.
validation_suggestions: Test interaction between CKD diagnosis and treatment assignment in trial data, adjusting for continuous eGFR to separate diagnosis effect from kidney function level.
Compare event and adverse event rates among CKD patients randomized to intensive vs standard targets in pooled analyses (e.g., SPRINT CKD subgroup).
Examine care-process differences (visit frequency, medication changes) by CKD status to see whether closer follow-up explains part of the interaction.
caveats: CKD diagnosis may reflect coding or care intensity differences rather than physiologic severity; it can act as a proxy for other unmeasured factors.
Apparent greater benefit could be primarily in absolute terms due to higher baseline risk; relative benefit may be similar.
CKD patients face higher risk of renal adverse events with intensive therapy; net benefit must weigh both.

cross_feature_patterns: Consistent theme: features marking higher baseline cardiovascular risk or greater achievable SBP reduction (older age, higher SBP, CKD/low eGFR) are associated with increased apparent benefit from intensive SBP lowering, while features that indicate vulnerability to coronary hypoperfusion or lower risk (low DBP, higher eGFR) attenuate benefit. Many interactions may reflect absolute-risk amplification rather than differences in relative efficacy; careful interaction testing and separation of absolute vs relative effects is recommended.
